# **AURUM\_v2\_Transcript\_Intelligence\_Report**

Project AURUM v1.0–v1.3 hit an information-theoretic and statistical wall because its core paradigm—serializing 35 continuous indicators into a \~330-token ASCII string, routing through a frozen English-language Qwen3-0.6B prelude, and training a 48-cell discrete barrier classifier with cross-entropy followed by an argmax expected-value (argmax-EV) decision rule—conflicts with three foundational principles of quantitative finance documented across institutional research1. First, text-tokenization degrades continuous metric geometry and cross-feature covariance before the network can apply volatility standardization or feature neutralization1. Second, training with classification cross-entropy decouples parameter updates from transaction-cost-adjusted portfolio utility, leaving the model blind to turnover drag and regime-dependent variance spikes (\[S01\], \[S05\], \[S02\])2. Third, evaluating an unshrunk argmax-EV policy across 48 barrier cells introduces severe selection bias under the False Strategy Theorem (\[S18\]): on 19,000 out-of-sample H1 bars with fat tails (skewness \-0.2, raw kurtosis 6.0), expanding the search space from 2 canonical cells to 48 cells inflates the required per-bar Sharpe hurdle from 0.0034 to 0.0146 (a 4.35x increase) and reduces the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) from a statistically significant 0.9525 to an indistinguishable-from-noise 0.54933. High-payoff barrier cells (such as ![][image1]) suffer the steepest out-of-sample degradation because multiplying a noisy tail-probability estimate ![][image2] by a large payoff ![][image3] scales estimation variance by ![][image4], causing the argmax operator to systematically select the most overestimated tail cell3.  
To re-architect AURUM v2.0 into an industrial-grade systematic XAUUSD engine within Kaggle's 2× Tesla T4 GPU constraints (15.6 GB VRAM each, \~25–30 GPU-hours/week) on your 16-year (2010–2025) M1/H1 dataset, the system should execute five architectural pivots grounded in primary evidence from the Oxford-Man Institute (\[S01–S08\]), Capital Fund Management (\[S09–S13\]), Man AHL (\[S22–S27\]), AQR/Yale (\[S14–S15\]), Hudson River Trading (\[S16\]), and Kaggle financial competition winners (\[S28–S31\])1:

> 1. **Replace 48-Cell Classification with Direct Cost-Aware Continuous Sizing:** Discard ASCII tokenization, the frozen LLM trunk, and the 48-cell softmax head. Map continuous, volatility-standardized numerical features directly to bounded risk weights ![][image5] scaled by ex-ante volatility ![][image6], optimizing a differentiable joint objective of Pooled Net Sharpe Ratio and a SoftMin worst-window penalty (a smooth proxy for Entropic Value-at-Risk, EVaR) using Two-Pass Exact Gradient Accumulation (\[S01\], \[S05\])2.  
> 2. **Enforce Compact, Regularized Capacity (6k–11k Parameters) Hybridized with GBDT:** On \~72k–88k training H1 bars, unregularized deep models overfit microstructure noise, which explains why AURUM's clean GBDT (+0.0487R) outperformed the v1.3 neural trunk (-0.0400R)6. Replace the 600M-parameter LLM with a 50/50 ensemble of your regularized GBDT and either a Jane-Street-style Bottleneck Denoising Autoencoder \+ Residual MLP (10,449 parameters, \[S28\]), an Oxford-Man Vectorized Variable Selection Network \+ GRU \+ 2-Head Attention DMN-Lite (6,129 parameters, \[S02, S05\]), or a ridge-shrunk Random Fourier Feature (RFF) timing head (\[S14\])1.  
> 3. **Hard-Code DST-Aware Gold/FX Fixing Clocks and Causal Cross-Asset Residualization:** Anchor M1-to-H1 path geometry to exact local exchange clocks—Tokyo FX Fix (09:55 JST), Shanghai Gold Exchange benchmark, LBMA Gold AM (10:30 London) and PM (15:00 London) auctions, ECB Fix (14:15 CET), COMEX open (08:20 ET), and WM/Reuters London 16:00 FX Fix (\[S35, S36, S37\])14. Strip common USD beta by causally residualizing XAUUSD against strictly lagged (![][image7] Directed Delay) EURUSD, USDJPY, XAGUSD, and FRED macro factors (\[S05, S16, S30\])6.  
> 4. **Embed Saturating Response Functions and Regime Changepoint Features:** Pre-transform multi-horizon trend signals (![][image8]) using CFM's saturating ![][image9] (![][image10], \[S09\]) or Man AHL's damped response ![][image11] (\[S26\]) so extreme extensions taper exposure before fundamentalist mean-reversion dominates11. Augment inputs with online Changepoint Detection severity (![][image12]) and location (![][image13]) scores over 21- and 126-bar lookbacks (\[S03, S04\])24.  
> 5. **Lock In Position Inertia Buffers, Drawdown Halving, and DSR Admission Gates:** Enforce Rob Carver's ±10% cost-scaled position inertia band around target weights (\[S22, S23\]), smooth model combination weights with a 125-period EWMA (\[S24\]), apply Man AHL's 50% risk-halving rule if portfolio drawdown breaches a time-varying threshold (\[S27\]), and block any candidate model from GPU deployment unless its out-of-sample DSR exceeds 0.95 under Purged K-Fold Cross-Validation (embargo \= 0.02, \[S17, S18\])4.

## **Part 2 — Institutional Microstructure and Session-Flow Wisdom**

Gold (XAUUSD) does not trade in a homogeneous 24-hour continuous diffusion. It trades across four distinct institutional liquidity regimes—Asian Physical (Shanghai/Tokyo), London Wholesale OTC (LBMA), US Futures (COMEX/Globex), and the Afternoon London/NY Overlap (LBMA PM \+ WMR 16:00 Fix)—each governed by scheduled benchmark auctions and balance-sheet handoffs15. Because AURUM v2.0 has 6 million M1 bars across XAUUSD, XAGUSD, EURUSD, and USDJPY, it can extract intra-hour M1 path geometry around these exact institutional clocks and feed them into the H1 decision engine without look-ahead.

### **2.1 The Intraday W-Shaped USD Cycle & FX Fixing Mechanics (\[S35, S36, S39, S44\])**

Krohn, Mueller, and Whelan (2024, *Journal of Finance*, \[S35\]) analyzed 20 years of intraday currency returns around the clock and documented a persistent **W-shaped intraday cycle in the U.S. Dollar** driven by institutional order imbalances around the three primary global FX fixes16. Between 17:00 EST (NY close) and 21:00 EST (just after the Tokyo Nakane fix at 09:55 JST), the USD portfolio (DOL) appreciates by **\+5.3% per annum (+2.1 bps/day, t-stat \= 12.0)** as Japanese importers and institutional hedgers execute net USD buy orders at the Tokyo reference rate, with activity surging on *Gotobi* days (the 5th, 10th, and month-end)15. Immediately after the Tokyo fix (21:00 EST to 02:00 EST), dealers unwind inventory and the USD reverses, depreciating by **\-5.5% per annum (-2.2 bps/day, t-stat \= 9.2)**16. Because Gold (XAUUSD) is dollar-denominated, this post-Tokyo USD depreciation (21:00–02:00 EST, coinciding with the Shanghai Gold Exchange morning session) provides a structural tailwind for XAUUSD during Asian hours16.  
A second major cycle unfolds during European and London hours (\[S35, S36\]). From 02:00 EST through 11:00 EST (spanning the ECB fix at 14:15 CET / 08:15 ET and the WM/Reuters 16:00 London fix, which is determined over a 5-minute window from 15:57:30 to 16:02:30 London time), the USD appreciates by **\+4.3% per annum (+1.7 bps/day, t-stat \= 4.1)**15. Immediately after the 16:00 London fix (11:00 EST to 17:00 EST NY close), the USD reverses and depreciates by **\-4.8% per annum (-1.9 bps/day, t-stat \= 5.5)**16. Crucially, individual currencies diverge after the London fix: while the Euro (EUR) appreciates strongly against the USD by **\+7.22%** and the Canadian Dollar (CAD) by **\+3.85%**, the Japanese Yen (JPY) is the sole major exception, depreciating against the USD by **\-2.95%**16. Consequently, EURUSD and USDJPY must be entered as separate lagged predictors in AURUM v2.0 rather than collapsed into a single static FX basket16. Furthermore, in the 30 minutes prior to scheduled US macroeconomic announcements (\[S39\]), informed trading generates pre-announcement drift accounting for **49%** of the total price adjustment in E-mini S\&P 500 futures and **39%** in 10-year Treasury note futures across the 7 strong-drift releases96.  
![][image210]

### **2.2 LBMA Gold AM/PM Auctions, Pre-Fix Drift, and the COMEX vs. London vs. SGE Hierarchy (\[S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43\])**

A common pitfall in retail and naive quant gold models is misunderstanding which venue leads price discovery and how scheduled auctions shape M1 path geometry. The empirical literature establishes a clear hierarchy separating peer-reviewed evidence from practitioner blog claims:

| Microstructure Dimension | Empirical / Econometric Reality (Strong Primary Evidence) | Practitioner Anecdote / Blog Claim (Weak or Contested) | Actionable Rule for AURUM v2.0 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **London OTC vs. COMEX Price Discovery (\[S37\])** | London OTC accounts for **78.0%–86.75%** of global gold turnover while COMEX accounts for **7.7%–9.89%**, yet **COMEX leads price discovery (Information Leadership Share)** on average across the 24h day since the 2006 Globex electronic upgrade due to centralization, leverage, and reduced microstructure noise17. | Bloggers often claim London physical wholesale or Asian physical flows dictate intraday price discovery103. | Weight US session macro/rates impulses (DGS10, T10YIE, SP500) heavily in cross-asset residualization17. |
| **Shanghai Gold Exchange (SGE / SHFE) Spillover (\[S41\])** | In China, SHFE futures account for **68.10%** of price discovery (Information Share) vs **31.90%** for SGE spot (AU T+D)102. However, Diebold-Yilmaz (DY12) spillover studies show SGE remains a **partially isolated market** due to vault restrictions; **COMEX and LBMA** are the dominant global net volatility spreaders101. | Opinion pieces (\[S43\], Kitco) claim Shanghai has "stolen the gold crown" and sets global prices overnight103. | Treat Asian hours (01:00–07:00 UTC) as a positive physical-accumulation drift regime (\[S40\]), not as a volatility-spillover leader98. |
| **LBMA AM (10:30) & PM (15:00) Auctions (\[S37, S38, S42\])** | Replaced the old teleconference fix on **March 20, 2015** with IBA electronic auctions running in **30-second rounds** at 10:30 and 15:00 London time95. Caminschi & Heaney (\[S38\]) show informed price drift, volume spikes, and volatility elevation begin **30 minutes before the 15:00 PM fix (14:30–15:00 London)**92. Weak evidence shows the PM fix shifts discovery slightly toward London, whereas the AM fix does not17. | — | Compute M1 cumulative return and signed volume imbalance strictly over 10:00–10:29 and 14:30–14:59 London local time as H1 bar inputs92. |
| **Overnight vs. US Daytime Return Asymmetry (\[S40, S43\])** | Blose, Gondhalekar & Kort (2018, \[S40\]) show across COMEX front futures, London Fix, and GLD that **overnight returns are significantly positive** while **US daytime returns are significantly negative** in both bull and bear gold markets98. Prices tend to open high and decline during the **first hour of trading**98. | Retail blogs (\[S43\]) attribute NY open drops to "central bank / bullion bank paper gold suppression" since Aug 5, 1993103. Joe Lucid (\[S43\]) critiques the suppression narrative via futures roll spreads, attributing drops to market-maker stop-runs in thin hours (e.g., after 04:00 ET)104. | Reject conspiracy narratives, but **encode the empirical regularity**: penalize unbuffered long breakouts at the COMEX open (08:00–09:00 ET) via an is\_comex\_first\_hour indicator98. |
| **US Macro News Pre-Release Drift vs. NFP Noise (\[S37, S39\])** | Kurov et al. (\[S39\]) show **49% of equity** and **39% of 10Y Treasury** announcement moves occur in \[t \- 30 min, t \- 5 sec\] before release96. Hauptfleisch et al. (\[S37\]) show US GDP and PPI releases boost COMEX price discovery, whereas **US Employment (NFP) increases overall market noise without increasing price discovery share**17. | Traders frequently try to trade directional breakouts in the first minute of NFP. | Use the \[08:00–08:29 ET\] M1 drift as a feature, but **widen the no-trade buffer during NFP hours** where noise spikes17. |

### **3.1 Why Recurrent Depth ![][image211] and Large Transformers Fail on \~75k Hourly Bars**

In AURUM v1.3, increasing recurrent loop depth ![][image211] failed to improve out-of-sample expectancy. The mined literature identifies three mathematical reasons for this failure. First, Majewski, Ciliberti, and Bouchaud (\[S10\]) demonstrate that high-frequency noise volatility ![][image116] is substantially larger than fundamental drift volatility ![][image22]20. When a recurrent layer iterates ![][image211] times without strict spectral contraction or Gated Linear Unit (GLU) suppression (\[S07\]), each recurrent pass amplifies ![][image116] nonlinearly, fitting sample-specific noise trajectories rather than underlying macro state transitions20. Second, even with 95,008 H1 bars (\~75,000 training bars), financial return features have a Spearman rank correlation ceiling around 0.05 (\[S29\])7. In TFT (\[S07\]) and Momentum Transformer (\[S02\]), the authors explicitly include **GLU gating with residual skip connections (GateAddNorm)** so the network can drive the sigmoid gate ![][image217], suppressing unnecessary nonlinear or recurrent contributions and collapsing back to a shallow linear pass when the signal-to-noise ratio is low9. Third, in Jane Street's 1st-place solution (\[S28\]), Yirun Zhang showed that an MLP trained on noisy financial features benefits from a **noisy bottleneck encoder** (GaussianNoise \+ BatchNorm \+ Swish) that must simultaneously reconstruct the input features (![][image218]) while passing a clean skip connection ![][image188] directly to the readout MLP12.

Per Research Rule 9, no complex neural architecture is recommended below without stating its exact inputs, outputs, loss function, parameter count, and why it complements or outperforms a regularized GBDT on \~72k–88k hourly bars. Even when evaluating multiple horizon or barrier structures, selecting an action via unshrunk ![][image237] amplifies estimation error. As Giuseppe Paleologo (\[S16\]) emphasizes, the estimation error on an expected return estimate is larger than the expected return itself18. For a high-payoff barrier cell with reward-to-risk ratio ![][image238], the breakeven hit rate is ![][image239], and the estimated expected value is ![][image240]. The variance of this expected value estimate scales quadratically with ![][image241] (\[INFERENCE\] from standard variance scaling):

Compare this to a canonical symmetric cell (![][image243]), where ![][image244]. Because the ![][image238] cell has **6.25x higher estimation variance** (and higher relative tail error because extreme events are sparse and sensitive to outliers, as Anthony Ledford notes in \[S25\]10), taking the maximum across 48 cells systematically selects the cell with the largest positive estimation error.  
AURUM v2.0 replaces 48-cell classification with **continuous position sizing** ![][image245] (\[S01, S05, S23\])2. ## **Part 4 — Risk, Turnover, and Execution Guardrails**

Small edges (+0.0487R per trade on GBDT) are eroded in production when unbuffered continuous forecasts churn positions on every H1 bar or when unscaled volatility spikes trigger correlated drawdowns. Below is the quantitative evidence from Rob Carver (\[S22, S23, S24\]), Man AHL (\[S25, S27\]), and Bailey & López de Prado (\[S18\]) that defines AURUM v2.0's execution and risk layer.

### **4.1 Turnover Mechanics and Position Inertia Buffering (\[S22, S23, S24, S33\])**

Rob Carver's empirical decomposition (\[S23\]) highlights an operational dynamic often overlooked in academic ML papers28. Even with a constant forecast (Long Only, 0.00 forecast turnover), continuously updating position sizes to match changing ex-ante volatility ![][image248] generates **2.53 turnovers per year** (reduced to **2.14** with a ±10% buffer)28. Moving from EWMAC 32 (8.92 buffered turnover) to EWMAC 4 (49.81 buffered turnover) increases trading activity by **5.58x**28. Furthermore, the proportional turnover reduction from a fixed ±10% position buffer is **\~30% on slow rules** (10.16 down to 7.04 on EWMAC 64), whereas fast rules (EWMAC 4\) cross the ±10% band so frequently that buffering alone only cuts position turnover by **\~5%** (52.63 to 49.81; a **17% total reduction** from the 61.80 forecast turnover), requiring an explicit **Dynamic Optimization (DO) cost penalty** alongside buffering to cut turnover by **one-third to one-half**28.  
Simultaneously, Carver's empirical comparison across four execution systems on the combined EWMACX forecast (\[S23\]) shows that **Continuous Forecast \+ Volatility Targeting (FV)** achieves a Sharpe Ratio of **1.18** and an unlevered CAGR of **25.8%** (with monthly skew of **1.41** and 5% lower tail ratio of **1.95**), outperforming **Binary \+ Volatility Targeting (BV)** (Sharpe **1.15**, CAGR **19.7%**, monthly skew **0.78**, lower tail ratio **1.47**), **Binary Non-Vol-Targeted Fixed Exit (1E1E)** (Sharpe **0.88**, CAGR **19.3%**, lower tail ratio **2.01**), and **Binary Non-Vol-Targeted Stop-Loss (1E1S)** (Sharpe **0.88**, CAGR **11.3%**, monthly skew **1.98**, lower tail ratio **1.62**)73. Carver finds that trading costs for volatility targeting would need to be **eight times higher** than actual backtested costs to neutralize FV's Sharpe and CAGR advantages73.  
![][image249]  
By combining DeePM's differentiable cost penalty (![][image16] during training, \[S05\]) with Carver's ±10% execution inertia band (\[S22, S23\]) and Hoffstein's fractional tranching (![][image250] or ![][image251] hours for non-urgent adjustments, \[S33\]), AURUM v2.0 suppresses both high-frequency model jitter and volatility-scaling micro-trades8. When trading costs widen (such as during the 17:00–18:00 ET Globex halt window, NFP release hours, or when VPIN exceeds its 90th percentile), AURUM v2.0 dynamically widens the inertia buffer half-width from ![][image252] according to the ratio of current effective cost ![][image253] to baseline cost ![][image254] (\[S22\], \[INFERENCE\] from Carver's cost-scaled buffer rule15):  
![][image255]

### **4.2 Drawdown Control, Non-Overlapping Accounting, and Multiple-Testing Deflation (\[S18, S25, S27\])**

To keep AURUM v2.0's maximum portfolio drawdown under 20% and prevent false strategy admission, we synthesize the quantitative rules from Man AHL (\[S25, S27\]) and Bailey & López de Prado (\[S18\]). On 19,000 out-of-sample H1 bars (assuming an observed annualized Sharpe of 1.20, sample skewness of \-0.2, raw kurtosis of 6.0, and cross-trial annualized Sharpe standard deviation of 0.50), expanding the selection pool from ![][image161] canonical cells to ![][image160] barrier cells raises the non-annualized hurdle ![][image30] from **0.0034** to **0.0146** and collapses the Deflated Sharpe Ratio from **95.25%** (passing the \>95% institutional gate) to **54.93%** (failing the gate)3. Simultaneously, Man AHL and Campbell Harvey (\[S27\]) show that for a strategy running at **10% annualized volatility** and a **0.50 annualized Sharpe ratio** over a 10-year window, the probability of reaching or exceeding a 1-sigma (**\-10%**) maximum drawdown is **97.1%**, a 2-sigma (**\-20%**) drawdown is **43.0%**, a 3-sigma (**\-30%**) drawdown is **9.9%**, and a 4-sigma (**\-40%**) drawdown is **1.5%**31.  
![][image256]

### **4.3 The Practitioner Risk & Execution Checklist**

> 1. **Zero Position Stacking (Single Net Exposure Ledger):** AURUM v1.3 suffered from overlapping multi-bar excursion accounting. In AURUM v2.0, the portfolio holds **at most one net position ![][image257] in XAUUSD at any timestamp ![][image112]** (\[S01, S05\])2. Multi-horizon signals (8h, 24h, 96h) are blended into a **single integrated forecast** (\[S23, S47\]) before computing target exposure ![][image258]8.  
> 2. **Target Volatility Cap (![][image259] Annualized) & Leverage Ceiling:** Because Man AHL's drawdown distribution (\[S27\]) shows a 43.0% 10-year probability of a 2-sigma drawdown at 0.50 Sharpe, setting annualized target volatility to 15% or 20% would make a 2-sigma drawdown equal \-30% to \-40%, breaching AURUM's \<20% max drawdown mandate31. Set ![][image260] annualized (approx. 0.129% per H1 bar) and hard-cap maximum notional leverage ![][image261].  
> 3. **Asymmetric Down-Move Volatility Scaling & Drawdown Risk-Halving (\[S25, S27\]):** Following Neil Shephard (\[S25\]), scaling exposure inversely with a responsive EWMA volatility estimator (halving exposure when local volatility doubles after a down-move) eliminates negative return skewness10. Following Man AHL (\[S27\]), implement a portfolio drawdown governor: if cumulative portfolio drawdown from the high-water mark reaches **\-10.0%** (or time-varying cutoff ![][image34]), multiply target exposure ![][image257] by **0.50** (50% risk reduction) until half of the drawdown loss is recovered (drawdown improves back above **\-5.0%**)31. Add a secondary circuit breaker at **\-18.0%** so max drawdown stays below 20%.  
> 4. **Surviving 2.0x Transaction Costs:** Train the neural trunk with ![][image16] (\[S05\])8, select hyperparameters on the validation set using net returns under **2.0x realistic transaction costs** (\[S02\])9, apply Carver's ±10% dynamic cost-scaled position inertia buffer (\[S22, S23\])28, and smooth model combination weights with a 125-period EWMA (\[S24\])29.

### **5.1 Blueprint 1: DST-Aware Fixing Clocks & Causal Cross-Asset Residualization (src/features/clock\_and\_residuals.py)**

Python  
import numpy as np  
import pandas as pd  
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

def build\_dst\_fixing\_and\_session\_features(m1\_df: pd.DataFrame) \-\> pd.DataFrame:  
    """  
    Aggregates M1 bars into H1 bars while extracting exact DST-aware institutional  
    fixing drift, last-hour order-flow reversal, and session handoff features.  
    Requires m1\_df with UTC DatetimeIndex and columns: \['open', 'high', 'low', 'close', 'volume'\].  
    """  
    idx\_utc \= m1\_df.index.tz\_convert("UTC")  
    idx\_ldn \= idx\_utc.tz\_convert(ZoneInfo("Europe/London"))  
    idx\_nyc \= idx\_utc.tz\_convert(ZoneInfo("America/New\_York"))  
    idx\_tyo \= idx\_utc.tz\_convert(ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo"))

    ret\_m1 \= np.log(m1\_df\["close"\] / m1\_df\["close"\].shift(1)).fillna(0.0)  
    tick\_sign \= np.sign(m1\_df\["close"\].diff()).replace(0.0, np.nan).ffill().fillna(0.0)  
    signed\_vol \= tick\_sign \* m1\_df\["volume"\]

    \# 1\. Pre-LBMA AM Fix \[10:00 \- 10:29 London\] & PM Fix \[14:30 \- 14:59 London\] 30-min drift  
    ldn\_mins \= idx\_ldn.hour \* 60 \+ idx\_ldn.minute  
    is\_pre\_lbma\_am \= (ldn\_mins \>= 600) & (ldn\_mins \< 630)  
    is\_pre\_lbma\_pm \= (ldn\_mins \>= 870) & (ldn\_mins \< 900)

    \# 2\. Pre-WMR London 16:00 Fix last-hour return & order-flow \[15:00 \- 15:59 London\]  
    is\_pre\_wmr\_lh \= (ldn\_mins \>= 900) & (ldn\_mins \< 960)

    \# 3\. Pre-US Macro Release 30-min drift window \[08:00 \- 08:29 NY\]  
    nyc\_mins \= idx\_nyc.hour \* 60 \+ idx\_nyc.minute  
    is\_pre\_us\_macro \= (nyc\_mins \>= 480) & (nyc\_mins \< 510)

    \# 4\. Variance Ratio Convexity Feature: (H1 displacement)^2 / sum(M1 return^2)  
    h1\_groups \= m1\_df.groupby(pd.Grouper(freq="1h"))  
    h1\_close \= h1\_groups\["close"\].last()  
    h1\_open \= h1\_groups\["open"\].first()  
    h1\_ret \= np.log(h1\_close / h1\_open)  
    m1\_rv \= ret\_m1.pow(2).resample("1h").sum()  
    vr\_convexity \= (h1\_ret.pow(2)) / (m1\_rv \+ 1e-12)

    \# Aggregate event-specific M1 drifts to H1 timestamp (strictly causal at end of H1 bar)  
    pre\_lbma\_am\_drift \= (ret\_m1 \* is\_pre\_lbma\_am).resample("1h").sum()  
    pre\_lbma\_pm\_drift \= (ret\_m1 \* is\_pre\_lbma\_pm).resample("1h").sum()  
    pre\_wmr\_lh\_ret \= (ret\_m1 \* is\_pre\_wmr\_lh).resample("1h").sum()  
    pre\_wmr\_lh\_ofi \= (signed\_vol \* is\_pre\_wmr\_lh).resample("1h").sum() / (  
        m1\_df\["volume"\].resample("1h").sum() \+ 1e-8  
    )  
    pre\_us\_macro\_drift \= (ret\_m1 \* is\_pre\_us\_macro).resample("1h").sum()

    \# Construct H1 DST-aware clock flags  
    h1\_idx\_ldn \= h1\_close.index.tz\_convert(ZoneInfo("Europe/London"))  
    h1\_idx\_nyc \= h1\_close.index.tz\_convert(ZoneInfo("America/New\_York"))  
    h1\_idx\_tyo \= h1\_close.index.tz\_convert(ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo"))

    features \= pd.DataFrame(index=h1\_close.index)  
    features\["vr\_h1\_m1\_convexity"\] \= vr\_convexity  
    features\["pre\_lbma\_am\_drift"\] \= pre\_lbma\_am\_drift  
    features\["pre\_lbma\_pm\_drift"\] \= pre\_lbma\_pm\_drift  
    \# Krohn-Mueller-Whelan (2024): negative sign on last-hour pre-fix return/OFI predicts post-fix reversal  
    features\["wmr\_post\_fix\_rev\_signal"\] \= \-1.0 \* pre\_wmr\_lh\_ret.shift(1).fillna(0.0)  
    features\["wmr\_post\_fix\_ofi\_signal"\] \= \-1.0 \* pre\_wmr\_lh\_ofi.shift(1).fillna(0.0)  
    features\["pre\_us\_macro\_drift"\] \= pre\_us\_macro\_drift

    \# Blose et al. (2018): Overnight positive vs US daytime (and COMEX 1st hour) negative asymmetry  
    features\["is\_us\_daytime"\] \= ((h1\_idx\_nyc.hour \>= 8) & (h1\_idx\_nyc.hour \< 17)).astype(np.float32)  
    features\["is\_comex\_first\_hour"\] \= (h1\_idx\_nyc.hour \== 8).astype(np.float32)  
    features\["is\_asian\_overnight"\] \= ((h1\_idx\_nyc.hour \>= 18) \| (h1\_idx\_nyc.hour \< 3)).astype(np.float32)

    \# Tokyo Gotobi Day Flag (5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th, or month-end in Tokyo)  
    is\_gotobi \= (h1\_idx\_tyo.day % 5 \== 0) \| (h1\_idx\_tyo.is\_month\_end)  
    features\["is\_tokyo\_gotobi\_pre\_fix"\] \= (is\_gotobi & (h1\_idx\_tyo.hour \== 9)).astype(np.float32)  
    features\["is\_london\_month\_end\_4pm"\] \= (  
        h1\_idx\_ldn.is\_month\_end & (h1\_idx\_ldn.hour \== 15)  
    ).astype(np.float32)

    return features

def causal\_cross\_asset\_residualizer(  
    xau\_ret: pd.Series,  
    cross\_Factor\_df: pd.DataFrame,  
    window: int \= 504,  
    ridge\_l2: float \= 1e-3,  
) \-\> pd.DataFrame:  
    """  
    Paleologo / DeePM Directed-Delay Causal Residualizer:  
    Estimates rolling beta using strictly prior window \[t \- window : t \- 1\]  
    and lagged t-1 cross-asset returns (EURUSD, USDJPY, XAGUSD, and forward-filled  
    daily FRED macro diffs) to prevent ragged-filtration look-ahead leakage.  
    """  
    X\_lag \= cross\_Factor\_df.shift(1).fillna(0.0).values  
    y \= xau\_ret.fillna(0.0).values  
    T, K \= X\_lag.shape

    idio\_resid \= np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)  
    rolling\_r2 \= np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)

    eye\_k \= ridge\_l2 \* np.eye(K)  
    for t in range(window, T):  
        \# Fit strictly on \[t \- window : t \- 1\] using Directed Delay (t-1) features  
        X\_win \= X\_lag\[t \- window : t\]  
        y\_win \= y\[t \- window : t\]  
        cov\_xx \= (X\_win.T @ X\_win) / window \+ eye\_k  
        cov\_xy \= (X\_win.T @ y\_win) / window  
        beta\_t \= np.linalg.solve(cov\_xx, cov\_xy)

        \# Residualize current return against strictly lagged t-1 factor impulse  
        idio\_resid\[t\] \= y\[t\] \- (X\_lag\[t\] @ beta\_t)

        var\_y \= np.var(y\_win) \+ 1e-12  
        var\_hat \= np.var(X\_win @ beta\_t)  
        rolling\_r2\[t\] \= np.clip(var\_hat / var\_y, 0.0, 1.0)

    out \= pd.DataFrame(index=xau\_ret.index)  
    out\["xau\_idio\_return\_t"\] \= idio\_resid  
    out\["xau\_idio\_vol\_ratio"\] \= np.sqrt(1.0 \- rolling\_r2)  
    return out

### **5.2 Blueprint 2: CFM Saturating Trend, Man AHL Damped MACD & Online Changepoint Features (src/features/regime\_and\_trend.py)**

Python  
import numpy as np  
import pandas as pd

def compute\_cfm\_and\_ahl\_trend\_features(close: pd.Series) \-\> pd.DataFrame:  
    """  
    Implements:  
    1\. CFM (Lemperiere et al. 2014\) saturating tanh trend signal (s\* \= 0.89).  
    2\. Man AHL (Baz et al. 2015\) multi-scale volatility-normalized MACD with  
       non-monotonic damped response R(y) \= y \* exp(-y^2 / 4\) / 0.89.  
    3\. Oxford-Man (Lim et al. 2019\) multi-horizon volatility-normalized returns.  
    """  
    df \= pd.DataFrame(index=close.index)  
    ret \= close.pct\_change().fillna(0.0)  
    \# 63-bar and 252-bar EWMA volatility and winsorization (Lim et al. 2019\)  
    ewm\_mean\_252 \= ret.ewm(halflife=252, min\_periods=20).mean()  
    ewm\_std\_252 \= ret.ewm(halflife=252, min\_periods=20).std().fillna(1e-4)  
    ret\_win \= ret.clip(lower=ewm\_mean\_252 \- 5.0 \* ewm\_std\_252, upper=ewm\_mean\_252 \+ 5.0 \* ewm\_std\_252)

    sigma\_t \= ret\_win.ewm(span=63, min\_periods=20).std().bfill() \+ 1e-8  
    df\["ex\_ante\_vol\_63"\] \= sigma\_t

    \# 1\. Multi-scale normalized returns: r\_{t-k, t} / (sigma\_t \* sqrt(k))  
    for k in \[1, 8, 24, 63, 126, 252\]:  
        ret\_k \= close.pct\_change(periods=k).fillna(0.0)  
        df\[f"norm\_ret\_{k}"\] \= (ret\_k / (sigma\_t \* np.sqrt(k))).clip(-5.0, 5.0)

    \# 2\. CFM Saturating Trend Signal: s^\* \* tanh(s\_n(t) / s^\*) with s^\* \= 0.89  
    s\_star \= 0.89  
    diff\_abs \= close.diff().abs().fillna(0.0)  
    for n in \[24, 96, 240\]:  
        p\_ema \= close.shift(1).ewm(span=n, min\_periods=10).mean()  
        sig\_n \= diff\_abs.shift(1).ewm(span=n, min\_periods=10).mean() \* np.sqrt(n) \+ 1e-8  
        s\_n \= (close.shift(1) \- p\_ema) / sig\_n  
        df\[f"cfm\_tanh\_trend\_{n}"\] \= s\_star \* np.tanh(s\_n / s\_star)

    \# 3\. Man AHL (Baz et al. 2015\) Damped MACD: (S, L) in \[(8, 24), (16, 48), (32, 96)\]  
    price\_std\_63 \= close.rolling(63, min\_periods=20).std().bfill() \+ 1e-8  
    macd\_damped\_list \= \[\]  
    for s\_span, l\_span in \[(8, 24), (16, 48), (32, 96)\]:  
        hl\_s \= np.log(0.5) / np.log(1.0 \- 1.0 / s\_span)  
        hl\_l \= np.log(0.5) / np.log(1.0 \- 1.0 / l\_span)  
        m\_s \= close.ewm(halflife=hl\_s, min\_periods=s\_span).mean()  
        m\_l \= close.ewm(halflife=hl\_l, min\_periods=l\_span).mean()  
        xi \= (m\_s \- m\_l) / price\_std\_63  
        xi\_std\_252 \= xi.rolling(252, min\_periods=30).std().bfill() \+ 1e-8  
        y\_k \= (xi / xi\_std\_252).clip(-4.0, 4.0)  
        \# Damped response function R(y) \= y \* exp(-y^2 / 4\) / 0.89  
        r\_y \= (y\_k \* np.exp(-0.25 \* (y\_k \*\* 2))) / 0.89  
        df\[f"ahl\_macd\_raw\_{s\_span}\_{l\_span}"\] \= y\_k  
        df\[f"ahl\_macd\_damped\_{s\_span}\_{l\_span}"\] \= r\_y  
        macd\_damped\_list.append(r\_y)

    df\["ahl\_macd\_composite"\] \= sum(macd\_damped\_list) / 3.0  
    return df

def fast\_causal\_changepoint\_features(ret: pd.Series, lbw\_list=(21, 126)) \-\> pd.DataFrame:  
    """  
    Fast vectorized CPU implementation of Oxford-Man (Wood et al. 2021\) Changepoint  
    Detection severity score nu\_t in (0, 1\) and normalized location gamma\_t in (0, 1).  
    """  
    r \= ret.fillna(0.0).values  
    T \= len(r)  
    out \= pd.DataFrame(index=ret.index)

    for l in lbw\_list:  
        nu \= np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float32)  
        gamma \= np.full(T, 0.5, dtype=np.float32)  
        for t in range(l, T):  
            win \= r\[t \- l : t \+ 1\]  
            std\_w \= np.std(win)  
            if std\_w \< 1e-12:  
                continue  
            z \= (win \- np.mean(win)) / std\_w  
            tss\_single \= np.sum(z \*\* 2)  
            best\_reduction \= 0.0  
            best\_c \= l // 2  
            cum\_sum \= np.cumsum(z)  
            cum\_sq \= np.cumsum(z \*\* 2)  
            for c in range(2, l \- 1):  
                n1, n2 \= c, (l \+ 1) \- c  
                rss1 \= cum\_sq\[c \- 1\] \- (cum\_sum\[c \- 1\] \*\* 2) / n1  
                sum2 \= cum\_sum\[-1\] \- cum\_sum\[c \- 1\]  
                sq2 \= cum\_sq\[-1\] \- cum\_sq\[c \- 1\]  
                rss2 \= sq2 \- (sum2 \*\* 2) / n2  
                reduction \= 0.5 \* (tss\_single \- (rss1 \+ rss2))  
                if reduction \> best\_reduction:  
                    best\_reduction \= reduction  
                    best\_c \= c  
            \# Wood et al. (2021) Eq. 10 logistic severity transformation  
            nu\[t\] \= 1.0 \- 1.0 / (1.0 \+ np.exp(-best\_reduction))  
            gamma\[t\] \= best\_c / float(l)

        out\[f"cpd\_severity\_{l}"\] \= nu  
        out\[f"cpd\_location\_{l}"\] \= gamma

    return out

### **5.3 Blueprint 3: Differentiable Cost-Aware Pooled \+ SoftMin Sharpe Loss With Two-Pass Exact Gradient Accumulation (src/losses/robust\_sharpe\_loss.py)**

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

class DeePMRobustSharpeLoss(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Oxford-Man DeePM (Wood, Roberts, Zohren 2026\) Joint Objective:  
    1\. Volatility-targeted net returns with explicit transaction cost scaler gamma.  
    2\. Pooled Net Sharpe Ratio \+ SoftMin worst-window penalty (EVaR proxy).  
    3\. Two-Pass Exact Gradient Accumulation for memory-constrained GPUs (Tesla T4).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(  
        self,  
        ann\_factor: float \= 6000.0,  
        cost\_bps: float \= 1.5,  
        gamma\_cost\_scaler: float \= 0.5,  
        softmin\_tau: float \= 0.2,  
        softmin\_lambda: float \= 0.25,  
        window\_len: int \= 120,  
        burn\_in: int \= 21,  
        eps: float \= 1e-8,  
    ):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.ann\_factor \= ann\_factor  
        self.cost\_rate \= cost\_bps \* 1e-4  
        self.gamma \= gamma\_cost\_scaler  
        self.tau \= softmin\_tau  
        self.lam \= softmin\_lambda  
        self.window\_len \= window\_len  
        self.burn\_in \= burn\_in  
        self.eps \= eps

    def compute\_net\_returns(  
        self,  
        raw\_actions: torch.Tensor,  
        vol\_scaled\_fwd\_returns: torch.Tensor,  
        ex\_ante\_vol: torch.Tensor,  
        sigma\_tgt: float \= 0.10 / (6000.0 \*\* 0.5),  
    ) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        """  
        raw\_actions: \[B, T\] pre-activation outputs  
        vol\_scaled\_fwd\_returns: \[B, T\] y\_{t+1} \= (sigma\_tgt / sigma\_t) \* r\_{t+1}  
        ex\_ante\_vol: \[B, T\] sigma\_t  
        """  
        p\_t \= torch.tanh(raw\_actions)  
        v\_t \= sigma\_tgt / (ex\_ante\_vol \+ self.eps)  
        w\_t \= v\_t \* p\_t

        \# Lagged notional exposure w\_{t-1} for exact turnover calculation  
        w\_prev \= torch.roll(w\_t, shifts=1, dims=1)  
        w\_prev\[:, 0\] \= 0.0  
        turnover \= torch.abs(w\_t \- w\_prev)

        r\_gross \= p\_t \* vol\_scaled\_fwd\_returns  
        r\_net \= r\_gross \- self.gamma \* self.cost\_rate \* turnover  
        \# Slice out burn-in steps L\_0 \= 21  
        return r\_net\[:, self.burn\_in :\]

    def forward(  
        self,  
        raw\_actions: torch.Tensor,  
        vol\_scaled\_fwd\_returns: torch.Tensor,  
        ex\_ante\_vol: torch.Tensor,  
    ) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        r\_net \= self.compute\_net\_returns(raw\_actions, vol\_scaled\_fwd\_returns, ex\_ante\_vol)  
        flat\_r \= r\_net.reshape(-1)

        \# 1\. Pooled Net Sharpe Loss  
        mean\_r \= torch.mean(flat\_r)  
        var\_r \= torch.mean(flat\_r \*\* 2) \- mean\_r \*\* 2 \+ self.eps  
        sr\_pool \= (mean\_r / torch.sqrt(var\_r)) \* (self.ann\_factor \*\* 0.5)  
        loss\_pool \= \-sr\_pool

        \# 2\. SoftMin Window Sharpe Penalty (EVaR Proxy)  
        B, T\_active \= r\_net.shape  
        if T\_active \>= self.window\_len:  
            n\_wins \= T\_active // self.window\_len  
            r\_wins \= r\_net\[:, : n\_wins \* self.window\_len\].reshape(-1, self.window\_len)  
        else:  
            r\_wins \= r\_net

        w\_mean \= torch.mean(r\_wins, dim=1)  
        w\_var \= torch.mean(r\_wins \*\* 2, dim=1) \- w\_mean \*\* 2 \+ self.eps  
        sr\_b \= (w\_mean / torch.sqrt(w\_var)) \* (self.ann\_factor \*\* 0.5)

        \# SoftMin over negative window Sharpe Z\_b \= \-SR\_b  
        z\_b \= \-sr\_b / self.tau  
        z\_max \= torch.max(z\_b).detach()  
        loss\_soft \= self.tau \* (  
            z\_max \+ torch.log(torch.mean(torch.exp(z\_b \- z\_max)) \+ self.eps)  
        )

        return loss\_pool \+ self.lam \* loss\_soft

def two\_pass\_exact\_sharpe\_step(  
    model: nn.Module,  
    loss\_fn: DeePMRobustSharpeLoss,  
    optimizer: torch.optim.Optimizer,  
    micro\_batches: list,  
) \-\> float:  
    """  
    Executes DeePM Two-Pass Exact Gradient Accumulation across micro-batches:  
    Pass 1 (no\_grad): Collects all micro-batch net returns and RNG states.  
    Pass 2 (with\_grad): Computes exact global pooled \+ SoftMin analytical gradients  
    with respect to each micro-batch's net return tensor and backpropagates.  
    """  
    optimizer.zero\_grad()  
    rng\_states \= \[\]  
    detached\_r\_list \= \[\]

    \# PASS 1: Statistical Accumulation (No Autograd)  
    for x\_m, y\_m, vol\_m in micro\_batches:  
        rng\_states.append(torch.get\_rng\_state())  
        with torch.no\_grad():  
            act\_m \= model(x\_m)  
            r\_net\_m \= loss\_fn.compute\_net\_returns(act\_m, y\_m, vol\_m)  
            detached\_r\_list.append(r\_net\_m.detach())

    \# Compute exact analytical upstream gradients dL / dR\_m across full logical batch  
    full\_r \= torch.cat(detached\_r\_list, dim=0).requires\_grad\_(True)  
    flat\_r \= full\_r.reshape(-1)  
    mean\_r \= torch.mean(flat\_r)  
    var\_r \= torch.mean(flat\_r \*\* 2) \- mean\_r \*\* 2 \+ loss\_fn.eps  
    loss\_pool \= \-(mean\_r / torch.sqrt(var\_r)) \* (loss\_fn.ann\_factor \*\* 0.5)

    z\_b \= \-((torch.mean(full\_r, dim=1) / torch.sqrt(torch.var(full\_r, dim=1, unbiased=False) \+ loss\_fn.eps)) \* (loss\_fn.ann\_factor \*\* 0.5)) / loss\_fn.tau  
    z\_max \= torch.max(z\_b).detach()  
    loss\_soft \= loss\_fn.tau \* (z\_max \+ torch.log(torch.mean(torch.exp(z\_b \- z\_max)) \+ loss\_fn.eps))  
    total\_loss \= loss\_pool \+ loss\_fn.lam \* loss\_soft  
    total\_loss.backward()

    upstream\_grads \= torch.split(full\_r.grad.detach(), \[r.shape\[0\] for r in detached\_r\_list\], dim=0)

    \# PASS 2: Analytical Gradient Injection (With Autograd & Replayed RNG)  
    for (x\_m, y\_m, vol\_m), rng\_st, g\_m in zip(micro\_batches, rng\_states, upstream\_grads):  
        torch.set\_rng\_state(rng\_st)  
        act\_m \= model(x\_m)  
        r\_net\_m \= loss\_fn.compute\_net\_returns(act\_m, y\_m, vol\_m)  
        r\_net\_m.backward(g\_m)

    torch.nn.utils.clip\_grad\_norm\_(model.parameters(), max\_norm=3.0)  
    optimizer.step()  
    return float(total\_loss.item())

### **5.4 Blueprint 4: Compact Continuous Trunks — Jane Street DAE-ResMLP (10,449 Params) & Oxford-Man DMN-Lite (6,129 Params) (src/models/continuous\_trunks.py)**

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn  
import torch.nn.functional as F

class JaneStreetDAEResMLP(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Yirun Zhang (gogo827jz) 1st Place Jane Street Bottleneck Denoising Autoencoder \+ Residual MLP,  
    adapted for continuous position sizing on D=48 features (Total verified params: 10,449).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_features: int \= 48, d\_enc: int \= 32, hidden\_dims=(64, 32), noise\_std: float \= 0.10):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.noise\_std \= noise\_std  
        self.bn\_in \= nn.BatchNorm1d(in\_features)

        \# Bottleneck Encoder & Decoder  
        self.enc\_dense \= nn.Linear(in\_features, d\_enc)  
        self.enc\_bn \= nn.BatchNorm1d(d\_enc)  
        self.dec\_drop \= nn.Dropout(0.15)  
        self.dec\_dense \= nn.Linear(d\_enc, in\_features)

        \# Auxiliary AE Readout  
        self.ae\_head \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(in\_features, d\_enc),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(d\_enc),  
            nn.SiLU(),  
            nn.Dropout(0.20),  
            nn.Linear(d\_enc, 1),  
        )

        \# Main Residual MLP Predictor (\[x0 \|\| z\] \-\> 64 \-\> 32 \-\> 1\)  
        self.cat\_bn \= nn.BatchNorm1d(in\_features \+ d\_enc)  
        self.cat\_drop \= nn.Dropout(0.20)  
        self.mlp\_block1 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(in\_features \+ d\_enc, hidden\_dims\[0\]),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden\_dims\[0\]),  
            nn.SiLU(),  
            nn.Dropout(0.25),  
        )  
        self.mlp\_block2 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(hidden\_dims\[0\], hidden\_dims\[1\]),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(hidden\_dims\[1\]),  
            nn.SiLU(),  
            nn.Dropout(0.25),  
        )  
        self.out\_action \= nn.Linear(hidden\_dims\[1\], 1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor):  
        orig\_shape \= x.shape  
        if x.dim() \== 3:  
            B, T, D \= orig\_shape  
            x\_flat \= x.reshape(B \* T, D)  
        else:  
            x\_flat \= x

        x0 \= self.bn\_in(x\_flat)  
        if self.training and self.noise\_std \> 0.0:  
            tilde\_x0 \= x0 \+ torch.randn\_like(x0) \* self.noise\_std  
        else:  
            tilde\_x0 \= x0

        z \= F.silu(self.enc\_bn(self.enc\_dense(tilde\_x0)))  
        x\_rec \= self.dec\_dense(self.dec\_drop(z))  
        ae\_act \= self.ae\_head(x\_rec)

        cat \= self.cat\_drop(self.cat\_bn(torch.cat(\[x0, z\], dim=-1)))  
        h1 \= self.mlp\_block1(cat)  
        h2 \= self.mlp\_block2(h1)  
        main\_act \= self.out\_action(h2)

        if len(orig\_shape) \== 3:  
            main\_act \= main\_act.reshape(B, T)  
            ae\_act \= ae\_act.reshape(B, T)  
            x\_rec \= x\_rec.reshape(B, T, D)  
        else:  
            main\_act \= main\_act.squeeze(-1)  
            ae\_act \= ae\_act.squeeze(-1)

        return main\_act, ae\_act, x\_rec

class GatedResidualNetwork(nn.Module):  
    """Exact Lim et al. (2021) / Wood et al. (2021) GRN with GLU and GateAddNorm."""  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, d\_model: int \= 16, dropout: float \= 0.15):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.fc1 \= nn.Linear(d\_model, d\_model)  
        self.fc2 \= nn.Linear(d\_model, d\_model)  
        self.drop \= nn.Dropout(dropout)  
        self.glu\_gate \= nn.Linear(d\_model, d\_model)  
        self.glu\_val \= nn.Linear(d\_model, d\_model)  
        self.norm \= nn.LayerNorm(d\_model)

    def forward(self, a: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        eta2 \= F.elu(self.fc1(a))  
        eta1 \= self.drop(self.fc2(eta2))  
        glu \= torch.sigmoid(self.glu\_gate(eta1)) \* self.glu\_val(eta1)  
        return self.norm(a \+ glu)

class OxfordManDMNLite(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Compact Vectorized Variable Selection \+ GRU \+ Masked 2-Head Attention \+ GRN  
    (Total verified params on D=48, d\_model=16: 6,129).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_features: int \= 48, d\_model: int \= 16, n\_heads: int \= 2, dropout: float \= 0.15):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.vsn\_gates \= nn.Linear(in\_features, in\_features)  
        self.vsn\_proj \= nn.Linear(in\_features, d\_model)  
        self.vsn\_grn \= GatedResidualNetwork(d\_model, dropout)

        self.gru \= nn.GRU(d\_model, d\_model, num\_layers=1, batch\_first=True)  
        self.mha \= nn.MultiheadAttention(d\_model, num\_heads=n\_heads, dropout=dropout, batch\_first=True)  
        self.glu\_att\_gate \= nn.Linear(d\_model, d\_model)  
        self.glu\_att\_val \= nn.Linear(d\_model, d\_model)  
        self.norm\_att \= nn.LayerNorm(d\_model)

        self.post\_grn \= GatedResidualNetwork(d\_model, dropout)  
        self.readout \= nn.Linear(d\_model, 1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        B, T, D \= x.shape  
        v\_weights \= F.softmax(self.vsn\_gates(x), dim=-1)  
        x\_selected \= x \* v\_weights  
        h\_vsn \= self.vsn\_grn(self.vsn\_proj(x\_selected))

        h\_gru, \_ \= self.gru(h\_vsn)  
        \# Strictly causal upper-triangular attention mask (tau \> t masked out)  
        causal\_mask \= torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)  
        att\_out, \_ \= self.mha(h\_gru, h\_gru, h\_gru, attn\_mask=causal\_mask)

        glu\_att \= torch.sigmoid(self.glu\_att\_gate(att\_out)) \* self.glu\_att\_val(att\_out)  
        h\_att \= self.norm\_att(h\_gru \+ glu\_att)  
        h\_final \= self.post\_grn(h\_att)  
        return self.readout(h\_final).squeeze(-1)

### **5.5 Blueprint 5: Carver ±10% Cost-Scaled Inertia Buffer, Man AHL Drawdown Halving, and DSR Admission Gate (src/execution/risk\_and\_execution.py)**

Python  
import numpy as np  
from scipy.stats import norm

def apply\_carver\_inertia\_buffer\_and\_dd\_control(  
    raw\_forecasts: np.ndarray,  
    ex\_ante\_vol: np.ndarray,  
    realized\_returns: np.ndarray,  
    cost\_multipliers: np.ndarray,  
    sigma\_tgt\_bar: float \= 0.10 / np.sqrt(6000.0),  
    base\_buffer\_frac: float \= 0.10,  
    dd\_half\_trigger: float \= 0.10,  
    dd\_recover\_trigger: float \= 0.05,  
    dd\_hard\_stop: float \= 0.18,  
    max\_leverage: float \= 2.0,  
) \-\> tuple\[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray\]:  
    """  
    Executes:  
    1\. Continuous volatility-targeted sizing w\*\_t \= (sigma\_tgt / sigma\_t) \* p\_t.  
    2\. Rob Carver's \+-10% Position Inertia Buffer dynamically scaled by cost\_multipliers.  
    3\. Man AHL (Harvey et al.) 50% Drawdown Risk-Halving state machine (\<20% Max DD cap).  
    """  
    T \= len(raw\_forecasts)  
    exec\_weights \= np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)  
    strat\_returns \= np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)  
    dd\_series \= np.zeros(T, dtype=np.float64)

    equity \= 1.0  
    hwm \= 1.0  
    risk\_scale \= 1.0  
    w\_prev \= 0.0

    for t in range(T):  
        \# Update drawdown state machine from prior realized equity  
        curr\_dd \= (hwm \- equity) / hwm  
        dd\_series\[t\] \= curr\_dd  
        if curr\_dd \>= dd\_hard\_stop:  
            risk\_scale \= 0.0  
        elif curr\_dd \>= dd\_half\_trigger:  
            risk\_scale \= 0.50  
        elif risk\_scale \== 0.50 and curr\_dd \<= dd\_recover\_trigger:  
            risk\_scale \= 1.00

        \# Target volatility-scaled position  
        v\_t \= sigma\_tgt\_bar / (ex\_ante\_vol\[t\] \+ 1e-8)  
        p\_t \= np.clip(raw\_forecasts\[t\], \-1.0, 1.0)  
        w\_star \= np.clip(risk\_scale \* v\_t \* p\_t, \-max\_leverage, max\_leverage)

        \# Dynamic \+-10% inertia buffer width scaled by current cost multiplier  
        avg\_pos \= risk\_scale \* v\_t \* 0.5  
        buf\_width \= base\_buffer\_frac \* avg\_pos \* max(1.0, cost\_multipliers\[t\])

        if w\_prev \< w\_star \- buf\_width:  
            w\_exec \= w\_star \- buf\_width  
        elif w\_prev \> w\_star \+ buf\_width:  
            w\_exec \= w\_star \+ buf\_width  
        else:  
            w\_exec \= w\_prev

        exec\_weights\[t\] \= w\_exec  
        if t \< T \- 1:  
            step\_ret \= w\_exec \* realized\_returns\[t \+ 1\]  
            strat\_returns\[t \+ 1\] \= step\_ret  
            equity \*= (1.0 \+ step\_ret)  
            if equity \> hwm:  
                hwm \= equity  
        w\_prev \= w\_exec

    return exec\_weights, strat\_returns, dd\_series

def evaluate\_deflated\_sharpe\_gate(  
    oos\_returns: np.ndarray,  
    trial\_sharpes\_non\_ann: np.ndarray,  
    n\_independent\_trials: int,  
) \-\> dict:  
    """  
    Bailey & Lopez de Prado (2014) Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) admission gate.  
    Requires DSR \> 0.95 to pass into production/GPU deployment.  
    """  
    T \= len(oos\_returns)  
    mu \= np.mean(oos\_returns)  
    sd \= np.std(oos\_returns, ddof=1) \+ 1e-12  
    sr\_obs \= mu / sd

    z\_scores \= (oos\_returns \- mu) / sd  
    skew \= float(np.mean(z\_scores \*\* 3))  
    kurt \= float(np.mean(z\_scores \*\* 4))

    emc \= 0.5772156649015329  
    var\_trials \= float(np.var(trial\_sharpes\_non\_ann, ddof=1)) if len(trial\_sharpes\_non\_ann) \> 1 else 0.0  
    if n\_independent\_trials \<= 1 or var\_trials \<= 0.0:  
        sr\_0 \= 0.0  
    else:  
        z1 \= norm.ppf(1.0 \- 1.0 / n\_independent\_trials)  
        z2 \= norm.ppf(1.0 \- 1.0 / (n\_independent\_trials \* np.e))  
        sr\_0 \= np.sqrt(var\_trials) \* ((1.0 \- emc) \* z1 \+ emc \* z2)

    se\_sr \= np.sqrt(max(1e-12, (1.0 \- skew \* sr\_obs \+ ((kurt \- 1.0) / 4.0) \* (sr\_obs \*\* 2)) / (T \- 1.0)))  
    z\_stat \= (sr\_obs \- sr\_0) / se\_sr  
    dsr \= float(norm.cdf(z\_stat))

    return {  
        "sr\_per\_bar": float(sr\_obs),  
        "sr\_annualized": float(sr\_obs \* np.sqrt(6000.0)),  
        "hurdle\_sr0\_per\_bar": float(sr\_0),  
        "se\_sr": float(se\_sr),  
        "skewness": skew,  
        "raw\_kurtosis": kurt,  
        "dsr\_probability": dsr,  
        "passes\_95\_gate": bool(dsr \> 0.95),  
    }

We flagged this discrepancy and implemented the bounded paper formula \[S03\].  
   * **Intermediate MACD Long Span (28 vs. 48):** Zohren's slide deck (\[S04\]) and the Medium TensorFlow article (\[S08\]) print the middle MACD pair as (16, 28\)27, whereas Baz, Granger, Harvey, Le Roux & Rattray (\[S26\]) and Lim, Zohren & Roberts (\[S01\]) define the geometric doubling series ![][image8]2. (16, 48\) maintains the consistent 3x long-to-short ratio across all three pairs and is used in Blueprint 2\.  
   * **Full GP Matérn 3/2 vs. Fast Likelihood Ratio Scan on 95k Bars:** Running GPflow Scipy optimization (MAX\_ITERATIONS \= 200 per kernel) across 95,008 H1 bars × 2 lookback windows requires ![][image267] L-BFGS iterations, which would stall CPU preprocessing26. In Blueprint 2, we provided an analytical two-regime Gaussian likelihood-ratio scan (fast\_causal\_changepoint\_features) that runs in seconds on CPU; Agent 1 should verify on CPU whether full GP Matérn 3/2 on downsampled H4/D1 bars adds incremental IC over the fast H1 scan.  
> 3. **Where Practitioner Anecdotes Conflict With Academic Evidence:**  
   * Retail/blog claims of "central bank paper gold manipulation at the COMEX open" (\[S43\]) conflict with futures roll spread analysis and information-share econometrics (\[S37, S43\])17. However, the **empirical pattern**—that gold returns during US daytime hours (especially the first hour of trading) are significantly negative on average (Blose, Gondhalekar & Kort 2018, \[S40\])—is documented in peer-reviewed literature98. AURUM v2.0 should encode the empirical time-of-day asymmetry while ignoring conspiracy narratives.

## **Executive Verdict — One-Page Action Plan for AURUM v2.0**

### **1\. What AURUM v2.0 Should Change Immediately (Architectural Mandates)**

* **Retire the v1.3 Paradigm:** Remove the \~330-token ASCII serializer, the frozen Qwen3-0.6B trunk, the 48-cell cross-entropy classification head, and the unshrunk argmax-EV selector. They suffer from quantization loss, cost-blindness, and a 4.35x multiple-testing hurdle penalty that drops DSR to 0.54932.  
* **Switch to Continuous Volatility-Targeted Sizing (FV) \+ ±10% Inertia Buffering:** Output a single continuous forecast ![][image5], scale by 63-bar EWMA volatility to target ![][image260] annualized volatility, and filter all position changes through Rob Carver's ±10% cost-scaled position inertia buffer with Man AHL's 50% drawdown risk-halving trigger at \-10% drawdown8.  
* **Train with Two-Pass Cost-Aware Pooled \+ SoftMin Sharpe Loss:** When training neural trunks on Tesla T4 GPUs, optimize DeePMRobustSharpeLoss (![][image16] training cost scaler, ![][image15] SoftMin temperature, ![][image76] burn-in steps) using two\_pass\_exact\_sharpe\_step so batch Sharpe variance gradients remain exact8.

### **2\. What Agent 1 Should Test Locally on CPU First (Before Touching Kaggle GPU Quota)**

> 1. **Step 1 (Execution Upgrade on Existing GBDT):** Apply apply\_carver\_inertia\_buffer\_and\_dd\_control and cfm\_saturating\_trend / ahl\_macd\_composite to your existing clean GBDT (+0.0487R) on CPU using Purged 5-Fold CV (embargo \= 0.02). Verify that turnover drops ≥20% and net expectancy survives 2.0x transaction costs22.  
> 2. **Step 2 (Microstructure & Residualization Lift):** Add build\_dst\_fixing\_and\_session\_features (pre-LBMA 30m drift, post-WMR 16:00 last-hour reversal, M1-to-H1 variance ratio convexity, Overnight vs US-Daytime flags) and causal\_cross\_asset\_residualizer (![][image7] lagged EURUSD, USDJPY, XAGUSD, and FRED macro series) on CPU. Retain only features that improve Purged CV Net Sharpe15.  
> 3. **Step 3 (Fast RFF-Ridge & Two-Pass Gradient Sanity Check):** Run RFFRidgeTimingModel (![][image262]) on CPU (\<10 seconds) and run the CPU unit test verifying two\_pass\_exact\_sharpe\_step matches single-batch autograd1. Only after Steps 1–3 pass and achieve ![][image156] should Agent 1 launch Kaggle 2×T4 GPU runs for JaneStreetDAEResMLP (10,449 params) and OxfordManDMNLite (6,129 params) blended 50/50 with the regularized GBDT (shrinkage\_SR \= 0.90, ewma\_span \= 125\)4.

### **3\. What AURUM v2.0 Should Ignore**

* **Ignore** LLM tokenization of numerical time series (\[S45\] shows 403 audited LLM trading strategies trailed random exposure-matched timing with ![][image43])107.  
* **Ignore** discrete multi-cell take-profit/stop-loss barrier grids (![][image160]) and binary stop-loss rules (1E1S), which Rob Carver showed trail continuous volatility-targeted sizing by 0.30 Sharpe units and \>14% CAGR4.  
* **Ignore** unregularized deep recurrent loops (![][image211]), unconstrained Reinforcement Learning (\[S21\]), and directional trading on raw VPIN (\[S19\])62.
